title: JESUS SAID LOOKING WITH LUST CAN BECOME ADULTERY OF THE HEART—WHAT DID HE MEAN?
paragraphs: JESUS SAID LOOKING WITH LUST CAN BECOME ADULTERY OF THE HEART—WHAT DID HE MEAN?
What if the sin nobody else can see is the very place where Jesus wants to set you free?
There are sins you can hide from your spouse.
Sins you can hide from your pastor.
Sins you can hide behind deleted history, locked phones, private messages, carefully managed social media accounts, and a reputation that still looks clean on Sunday morning.
But there is one place you cannot hide them.
The heart.
And that is exactly where Jesus went.
“Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not commit adultery:
But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.”
—Matthew 5:27–28, KJV
Those words have frightened people.
Convicted people.
Confused people.
And sometimes they have even been used carelessly, leaving sincere believers wondering whether noticing that another human being is attractive means they have already committed adultery.
But Jesus was saying something far deeper than that.
And understanding what He actually said may expose something uncomfortable in you.
It may also lead you toward freedom.
The Greek wording matters.
Matthew 5:28 reads in part:
πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν
pas ho blepōn gynaika pros to epithymēsai autēn
The crucial expression is πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν—pros to epithymēsai autēn.
Jesus is describing looking directed toward desire—looking in order to lust, covet, or desire.
That distinction matters.
Jesus was not teaching that recognizing physical beauty is automatically adultery.
He was not saying that every involuntary temptation makes you an adulterer.
He was not declaring that the first unwanted thought entering your mind is morally identical to choosing to entertain it.
Scripture itself distinguishes temptation from consenting to sin. Jesus Himself “was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15).
Temptation and sin therefore cannot simply be identical.
James describes desire conceiving and then giving birth to sin (James 1:14–15). There is movement. There is enticement. There is consent.
Jesus is confronting the heart that does not merely notice but deliberately looks in order to desire.
The gaze that stays because it wants something.
The imagination that takes another human being and privately turns that person into an object for sexual possession.
The heart that says:
Nobody knows.
Nobody sees.
I'm not touching anyone.
So technically, I'm still clean.
Jesus destroys that hiding place.
Not because He hates you.
Because He loves you too much to let outward respectability become camouflage for inward slavery.
The religious world around Jesus knew the seventh commandment:
“Thou shalt not commit adultery.”
But Jesus takes His listeners beneath the visible act and into the place from which the act can grow.
The heart.
This is characteristic of the Sermon on the Mount.
Jesus does something similar with murder. He moves from the external act of killing into anger and contempt (Matthew 5:21–22).
Then He moves from adultery into lust.
Why?
Because the kingdom of God is not merely interested in keeping your hands from committing certain acts while leaving your heart untouched.
Jesus wants the heart.
That means Christianity cannot be reduced to:
“I never slept with her.”
“I never touched him.”
“I never physically cheated.”
“I only watched.”
“I only imagined.”
“I only messaged.”
“My spouse doesn't know.”
“It wasn't technically adultery.”
Jesus walks straight through the word technically and asks:
What is happening inside your heart?
That question hurts because some people reading this have remained physically faithful while privately cultivating an entire secret sexual world.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you have never crossed the physical line.
Maybe the person sleeping beside you thinks everything is fine.
Maybe you worship.
Maybe you serve.
Maybe you preach.
Maybe you post Bible verses.
And maybe there is another version of you that appears when the door closes and the screen lights up.
Jesus sees both versions.
And here is where many people expect condemnation to be the end of the story.
It isn't.
Because the same Jesus who exposes darkness is the Jesus who came to rescue people from it.
Listen to what He says next:
“And if thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out, and cast it from thee... And if thy right hand offend thee, cut it off, and cast it from thee...”
—Matthew 5:29–30, KJV
Those words sound terrifying if ripped away from their context.
Jesus is using deliberately shocking language to communicate the deadly seriousness of sin.
He is not establishing self-mutilation as the cure for lust.
Think about it.
Removing an eye cannot remove lust from the heart.
Removing a hand cannot purify desire.
Jesus has already located the battlefield.
The heart.
The force of His words is this:
Do not negotiate with the sin that is destroying you.
Take radical action.
If something repeatedly becomes an avenue into sin, stop treating access to it as more precious than holiness.
Maybe for you that means deleting something.
Blocking someone.
Ending a conversation.
Installing accountability.
Confessing to a mature believer.
Changing what you watch.
Refusing to revisit the account you know awakens fantasies.
Stopping the private messages you keep calling “innocent” even though you know exactly why you wait for them.
Putting the phone outside the bedroom.
Getting pastoral help.
Seeking professional help where compulsive sexual behavior has become deeply entrenched.
Not because these actions purchase salvation.
They don't.
But repentance does not keep making comfortable arrangements with the thing from which it claims to be turning.
There is another truth we desperately need here.
Sexual desire itself is not evil.
God created human sexuality.
Marriage is honorable, and Scripture speaks positively of marital intimacy. The problem Jesus identifies is not that human beings possess sexual desire.
The problem is desire distorted into coveting and consuming someone who is not yours to possess.
Lust takes a person made in the image of God and reduces that person to something existing for your private gratification.
Love asks:
“How can I honor this person before God?”
Lust asks:
“How can this person satisfy me?”
Love sees a whole human being.
Lust can turn a human being into a body.
Love seeks another person's good.
Lust is willing to consume another person inside the imagination even when that person never knows it happened.
And suddenly Jesus' teaching becomes much bigger than a rule about where your eyes point.
He is confronting the way you see people.
That woman on the screen is somebody's daughter.
That man in your fantasy bears God's image.
That married coworker is not an escape from the problems in your marriage.
That person you keep stalking online is not a character God placed inside your private imagination for your consumption.
People are not pornography.
People are not fantasies.
People are image-bearers.
And Jesus wants to restore your eyes until you can see them that way again.
But perhaps you have already failed.
Perhaps that is why you are still reading.
Maybe this isn't theological curiosity for you.
Maybe you know exactly what Jesus is talking about.
You promised God you would stop.
Then you went back.
You cried afterward.
Deleted everything.
Prayed.
Lasted three days.
Maybe three weeks.
Then something happened.
Loneliness.
Stress.
A fight with your spouse.
A memory.
A recommendation on your feed.
A late night when nobody was watching.
And suddenly you were back in the same place, asking God how many times He could possibly forgive the same person for the same thing.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is not:
“Clean yourself up enough and perhaps Jesus will accept you.”
The Gospel is that sinners who cannot make themselves righteous are invited to come to Christ.
Jesus did not die for imaginary people who never needed forgiveness.
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
—Romans 5:8, KJV
That does not make sin small.
The cross proves exactly the opposite.
Sin is so serious that redemption required the blood of Christ.
But grace is so astonishing that Christ willingly gave Himself for sinners.
This is where conviction and condemnation must not be confused.
Conviction brings darkness into the light and calls you home.
Condemnation whispers:
Hide.
Pretend.
You're disgusting.
God doesn't want you anymore.
Never let anyone know.
But Jesus says:
Come into the light.
Repent.
Bring Me what you have been hiding.
There is forgiveness here.
There is cleansing here.
There is a new way to live.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
—1 John 1:9, KJV
Not some unrighteousness.
All unrighteousness.
Maybe your scandal has never become public.
Maybe it exists entirely inside your browser history and memory.
Maybe the scandal is in your heart.
But grace can reach there too.
That is why repentance matters.
Biblical grace is not Jesus saying, “It doesn't matter.”
Grace is Jesus meeting guilty people where they are and refusing to leave them enslaved there.
Remember the woman caught in adultery in John 8.
Jesus did not join the mob demanding her destruction.
Neither did He redefine adultery as harmless.
His words hold mercy and transformation together:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.”
Grace.
Then transformation.
Forgiveness.
Then a new road.
That is Christianity.
And perhaps the most frightening thing about lust is not simply what happens while you are looking.
It is what repeated looking can slowly train your heart to become.
What you repeatedly feed can begin shaping what you repeatedly desire.
What you repeatedly normalize can stop shocking your conscience.
And eventually the thing you once resisted can become the thing you defend.
That is why Jesus speaks urgently.
Not because He wants miserable Christians terrified of their own humanity.
Because He knows where unchecked sin leads.
He is not trying to steal pleasure from you.
He is trying to rescue you from being mastered by desire.
Somebody needs to hear this:
You do not have to keep living two lives.
You do not have to worship Jesus publicly while surrendering to lust privately.
You do not have to become perfect tonight.
But you do need to stop calling darkness harmless simply because nobody else can see it.
Bring it into the light.
Tell Jesus the truth.
He already knows.
If necessary, tell a trustworthy mature Christian who will pray with you, challenge you, and refuse to help you hide.

If you are married and your behavior has crossed boundaries that affect your spouse, seek wise pastoral or professional guidance about truthful confession and restoration rather than continuing deception.
And when temptation returns—and temptation may return—remember something enormously important:
The presence of temptation is not proof that Christ has abandoned you.
Fight.
Flee.
Pray.
Redirect your eyes.
Renew your mind with Scripture.
Remove access where necessary.
Get back up when you fall.
Keep bringing your heart to Christ.
Not to earn His blood.
Because His blood is your only hope.
There is no shame in admitting that you need prayer.
Someone reading the comments tonight may desperately need proof that failure does not have to be the final chapter.
Send this article to someone who is fighting quietly.

Supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical way to help biblical teaching reach more people. But supporting a ministry does not earn God's favor, prove your faith, purchase blessing, or make you more acceptable to Him. Christ alone saves, and everything we give should flow freely from love for God rather than spiritual pressure.
And beyond supporting the work, stay because you want to keep growing.
But before you leave this page, return once more to the words of Jesus.
“Whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.”
He was not merely raising the standard until nobody could survive.
He was tearing away our favorite illusion:
That righteousness is only about what other people can prove we did.
Jesus goes deeper.
Into motives.
Into imagination.
Into desire.
Into locked rooms.
Into hidden tabs.
Into secret conversations.
Into the places where everyone else thinks you are innocent because nobody else has been allowed inside.
And astonishingly...
He goes there not merely to expose you.
He goes there to redeem you.
The Christian story is not the story of spotless people congratulating themselves for never struggling.
It is the story of sinners being washed, forgiven, transformed, sanctified, and taught to walk in the light because Jesus Christ died and rose again.
So when your eyes wander, bring your heart back.
When desire tries to become possession, surrender it.
When temptation whispers, flee toward Christ.
When you fall, repent instead of hiding.
When shame tells you to disappear, remember the cross.
And when Satan tries to convince you that your secret failure has become your permanent identity, remember whose name was written over your redemption.
Jesus.
Your worst hidden chapter does not have to become the title of your life.
The Savior who sees what nobody else sees is still able to redeem what nobody else knows is broken.
